name: Central Market
label: Central Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jalan Hang Kasturi' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Jalan Hang Kasturi nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Art deco market building selling crafts and souvenirs.

text.description: Central Market began in 1888 as a wet market, and the Art Deco building you see today was finished in 1937. It was saved from demolition and later renovated in 1985–86, then relaunched as Pasar Budaya (the Cultural Market). That history gives you plenty to photograph: a light-blue facade, long rows of stalls and a lively street scene. From there, look north towards the market, which sits with the covered pedestrian-only section of Jalan Hang Kasturi to the north. Walk about 300 m north to reach that covered walkway, which has food and drink kiosks and stalls, so the photo is full of colour, signs and people. This stretch links to Kasturi Walk, opened in 2011, which is known for snack and souvenir stalls and for street musicians. If you want the classic view of the building itself, the front entrance, with the drop-pin sculpture in the foreground, is the alternative angle. Kasturi Walk, nearby, suits a wider street scene with the market in the background. On a phone, the covered walkway works well because the roof frames the shot and leads the eye along the street. Keep your phone steady, wait for a gap in the crowd, and ask stall owners before taking close-ups of people or their goods. Check the front of the building for works or barriers before you plan a facade shot.
text.geographic_location: Central Market is in central Kuala Lumpur, on Jalan Tun Tan Cheng Lock and the pedestrian-only part of Jalan Hang Kasturi, next to the Klang River and a few minutes from Petaling Street.
text.directions_text: Head for the Petaling Street area and walk towards the Klang River; the market is only a few minutes from there. The Pasar Seni station, named after the market, is close by. The covered pedestrian street, Jalan Hang Kasturi, is reached by walking north from there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the covered walkway. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full length of the street and the roof. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as signs and stall displays.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jalan Hang Kasturi (covered pedestrian section beside the market). The covered walkway with kiosks and stalls running along the side of the market building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the walkway so it runs towards the middle of the frame, with the stalls on either side. Keep the phone level so the roofline stays straight. For a different view, try the market's front entrance with the drop-pin sculpture in the foreground, or walk along Kasturi Walk for a wider street scene with the market in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright area of the street to set focus and exposure, then use the exposure slider to bring back detail if the covered part looks dark. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of people walking through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go earlier in the day for fewer people in the walkway. The roof gives some cover from sun and rain, so the spot works in most weather.

text.access_note: The pedestrian street is open public space, but the market building and its shops have their own opening times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Petronas Towers
label: Petronas Towers
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'KLCC Park' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'KLCC Park' (way/10590000): edge nearest the subject (680 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/279944536: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Petronas Towers' (201 m across).
notes: Iconic twin skyscrapers and the symbol of Kuala Lumpur.

text.description:
The Petronas Towers are a pair of 88-storey towers linked by a sky bridge, standing 451.9 m tall. From 1998 to 2004 they were the tallest buildings in the world, and they are still the tallest twin towers. They were officially opened on 31 August 1999 on the site of the old Selangor Turf Club race track. The steel and glass skin is designed to echo patterns from Islamic art.

For a phone photo, the classic spot is KLCC Park, on the lake side, looking at the towers across the water. From here you can fit both towers into one upright frame, with the park's greenery and fountain area around them. If the water is calm, the towers also appear as a reflection. Visitor guides recommend the lake edge for exactly this view, and it is free to stand there.

The best light is blue hour, when the sky is deep blue and the towers are lit. Arrive before sunset, because the walkways can get busy and the best places at the water's edge fill up. If you want a different view, the Pintasan Saloma pedestrian and bicycle bridge shows the towers above the city, with the lit bridge structure in the foreground at night.
text.geographic_location: The towers stand in Kuala Lumpur, above the Suria KLCC shopping mall.
text.directions_text: Head for the KLCC area and KLCC Park, near the towers. According to visitor guides, the park can be reached on foot from KLCC station. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) and hold the phone upright, so both towers fit with some water and greenery below them. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the water and want more of the park around the towers. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the towers' upper floors and the sky bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in KLCC Park (lake side of the park, facing the towers across the water). Both towers framed by the lake, park greenery and fountain area, with the towers' reflection in calm water. For the classic across-the-water view recommended by visitor guides, walk to the lake edge in KLCC Park. From there you see both towers framed by the lake, the park greenery and the fountain area, with the towers' reflection in calm water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the towers with the vertical lines, so they stand straight. Keep the phone level rather than tilting it upwards. At the lake edge, put the water in the lower part of the frame so the reflection fills the foreground. For a different shot, try the Pintasan Saloma bridge, which gives a view of the towers over the city with the bridge's lit structure in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the towers to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the lit towers do not turn white. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows or the phone on a solid ledge to keep it steady. At the lake, wait for a moment when the water is calm for the best reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour: from about 30 to 60 minutes before sunset until full darkness. Arrive before sunset to get a good spot.

text.access_note: KLCC Park is an open public space where, according to visitor guides, you can stand without a ticket, but check the official site before you go for closures, photography rules, and any visits inside the towers.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting a phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean inwards.
Resting a phone on a solid ledge helps keep night-mode shots steady.
Dragging the exposure slider down keeps bright lit buildings from looking washed out.

name: Batu Caves
label: Batu Caves
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ramayana Cave' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ramayana Cave' (node/1686530074): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1362025121: large area 'Batu Caves பத்து மலை' (638 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Limestone hill with a huge golden statue and rainbow stairs.

text.description: Batu Caves is a limestone hill about 13 km north of central Kuala Lumpur, with a group of Hindu temples built into its caves. It photographs well because the colour is so concentrated: a 42.7 m golden Murugan statue, a rainbow-painted staircase of 272 concrete steps (built in 1940 and repainted in 2018) and a sheer limestone cliff behind. The hill is about 325 m tall, and the temple to Murugan sits in the largest cave. From there you can photograph the 15 m Hanuman statue and the Hanuman temple (opened November 2001), along with the painted figures around the cave entrance. It is often quieter here than at the foot of the main staircase, and it gives you colourful detail shots instead of the usual wide view. Monkeys are common around the steps and forecourt, so keep your phone and food close. Thaipusam brings very large crowds to the forecourt. Photography inside the caves is restricted, with no flash and no drones, so ask permission before photographing worshippers.
text.geographic_location: Batu Caves is in Gombak, Selangor, about 13 km north of central Kuala Lumpur.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed for this spot; head north from central Kuala Lumpur towards Batu Caves in Gombak. Once you are at the foot of the hill, find the main staircase and walk to its left, where the Hanuman statue and Ramayana Cave stand. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Hanuman statue and the painted figures. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the statue and the cave entrance together in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as faces, paintwork and the staircase. It also keeps you at a respectful distance from the monkeys.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Ramayana Cave (outside the entrance, beside the Hanuman statue at the foot of the hill, left of the main staircase). The large green Hanuman statue and the painted, colourful sculptures around the cave entrance. From here you see the large green Hanuman statue and the colourful painted sculptures around the cave entrance. It is a quieter, less crowded place to shoot than the main staircase.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the Hanuman statue upright, with the painted figures filling the lower corners of the frame. Then step back for a wider shot that includes the cave entrance. For a different view, the Lord Murugan statue is an alternative: it shows the golden figure, the rainbow staircase and the cliff together in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright paint and sky do not wash out. Do not use flash near the cave or inside it, as it is not allowed.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No best time is given for this spot. As general advice, softer light earlier or later in the day is kinder to bright painted colours than harsh midday sun. Avoid Thaipusam if you want an uncrowded frame, though it is a very busy time for the festival itself.

text.access_note: The outdoor forecourt and the Hanuman statue are free to stand in front of, but this is a working place of worship and parts of the site may be ticketed or have restricted hours, so check the official site before you go.

name: Perdana Botanical Gardens
label: Perdana Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sunken Garden' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Sunken Garden' (way/776280263): middle (76 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/111547419: large area 'Perdana Botanical Gardens' (1425 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Large green park with lakes and gardens west of the centre.

text.description: Perdana Botanical Gardens is Kuala Lumpur's first large recreational park, covering 91.6 hectares close to the city centre. It was started in 1888 by Alfred Venning, the British State Treasurer of Selangor, who had a stream dammed to make the ornamental lake. The gardens were formally opened on 13 May 1889. With a park this big, the best approach for a phone is to pick one corner and do it well. The Sunken Garden is the one to choose. It is a circular lawn set down in a bowl, with an eight-pointed star fountain, white flower pots and neatly clipped hedges. Guides call it the most photogenic spot in the gardens. Stand at the hedge arch at the garden's entrance and look down into the bowl. The arch frames the view and gives it a secret-garden feel, and the fountain gives your eye somewhere to land. The shape of the lawn and the hedges also makes the picture look tidy and balanced without much effort. If you have time for a second picture, Laman Perdana has a wavy yellow metal-and-glass canopy against the greenery. Cycad Island has a bamboo playhouse with water in front of it. The park also holds the Orchid Garden, the Hibiscus garden, the deer park, the Bird Park and the Butterfly Park, so it is easy to fill a few hours.
text.geographic_location: The gardens sit in the heart of Kuala Lumpur, along Jalan Perdana (also known as Venning Road), close to the National Museum of Malaysia.
text.directions_text: The gardens lie along Jalan Perdana, near the National Museum of Malaysia. Muzium Negara MRT station is the nearest public transport hub to the gardens, within walking distance of the park, though it is not close to the Sunken Garden stand-here point. Once inside, follow the paths and use the map to reach the Sunken Garden. It is a big park, so allow extra walking time. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which suits the framed view through the arch. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole bowl, or to 2x telephoto to pick out the fountain and the flower pots.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (from the hedge arch at the garden's entrance, looking down into the bowl). The circular sunken lawn with its eight-pointed star fountain, white flower pots and clipped hedges, framed by the arch. Look down into the bowl. You should see the circular lawn, the star-shaped fountain, the white flower pots and the clipped hedges, all framed by the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the arch's edges straight along them, so the hedge makes a neat frame around the lawn. Place the fountain at the centre or on a crossing of the grid lines. If you have time, Laman Perdana's yellow canopy and the bamboo playhouse on Cycad Island make good alternative pictures elsewhere in the park.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the fountain or the lawn to set focus. Then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or the sunlit grass looks washed out. Take a couple of shots at different zoom levels so you can pick the best one later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, according to one guide, when the light is best here.

text.access_note: The gardens are a public park, but opening times and fees for some areas (a weekend fee may apply to the Orchid and Hibiscus gardens) and any permit for commercial photography or drones can vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Merdeka 118
label: Merdeka 118
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Old Kuala Lumpur Street Art' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'The St. Regis Kuala Lumpur' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/645604854: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Merdeka Maybank Tower' (78 m across).
notes: Supertall skyscraper with a faceted crown.

text.description: Merdeka 118, now officially renamed Merdeka Maybank Tower, is the tallest building in Malaysia and the second tallest in the world, at 678.9 metres across 118 storeys. It rises over the Merdeka area on the edge of Chinatown, so it makes a strong backdrop to older streets and rooftops. The tall, tapering shape suits phone photos taken in portrait orientation. The glass is cut into diamond-shaped panels, a pattern meant to reflect Malaysia's variety of people. The overall shape is said to echo Tunku Abdul Rahman's raised hand as he called out "Merdeka!" at independence in 1957. The structure was completed in November 2023, and the Park Hyatt hotel in the upper floors began operating in August 2025. The wider complex was still unfinished and mostly closed to visitors at the time of the latest information, so plan on photographing it from outside. The most popular angle is from the alleyway known as Old Kuala Lumpur Street Art in Chinatown. There, the tower stands above the painted walls and shophouse roofs, which gives the picture a sense of scale. Go early in the morning, because the alley gets busy. For a different view, the forecourt at the foot of the tower (Linear Park) shows its full height from the ground, and Taman Rekreasi Pudu Ulu shows it from across the park's greenery at sunrise or golden hour.
text.geographic_location: Merdeka 118 stands in the Merdeka area of central Kuala Lumpur, just beside Chinatown and Petaling Street and close to Merdeka Stadium.
text.directions_text: Search Old Kuala Lumpur Street Art on Google Maps to find the alleyway in Chinatown. If you would rather go to the base of the tower, it has its own Merdeka MRT station on the Kajang Line. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) in the alley, so the street art and buildings stay in the picture and the tower sits above them. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move to the forecourt at its base.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Old Kuala Lumpur Street Art (alleyway in Chinatown; find it by searching this name on Google Maps). The tower framed above the alley's street art and the Chinatown buildings. From here the tower is to the north-east, above the painted walls and Chinatown buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone upright and turn on gridlines. Put the alley's street art in the lower part of the frame and let the tower rise through the upper part. Keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean. At the forecourt of the tower (Linear Park), use ultra-wide and tilt up to fit its full height against open sky. Taman Rekreasi Pudu Ulu is a good alternative for a wider view with greenery in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the glass. Take a few frames, as people may walk through the alley.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the alley is said to be less busy. Sunrise or golden hour also suits the Pudu Ulu view. After dark the tower is lit, so try night mode.

text.access_note: The alley is a public street, but the tower and its observation areas may be closed or ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting a phone upwards makes tall buildings look as if they lean inwards, so keeping it level reduces this.
A telephoto lens (2x-5x) makes a distant tower look larger compared with the buildings in front of it.
Night mode can help with photos of the tower's lights after dark.
Tapping to focus and lowering the exposure helps keep bright sky from washing out detail in the glass.

name: Bukit Bintang
label: Bukit Bintang
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jalan Bukit Bintang pedestrian crossing near Pavilion' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Jalan Bukit Bintang and Jalan Sultan Ismail (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Bukit Bintang'.
notes: Main shopping and nightlife district, lively at night.

text.description: Bukit Bintang is Kuala Lumpur's main shopping and entertainment district, and the busiest stretch of it is a gift for street photography after dark. Jalan Bukit Bintang itself is about 3.4 km long, and the district takes its name from a hill of roughly 50 m that once stood nearby. Today the scene is malls, cafés, bars and food streets. Pavilion was built in late 2007 and is a seven-storey mall, so its lit frontage makes a bright backdrop behind the crowds. From here you can catch people crossing, the trails of passing traffic and neon signs all in one frame. A travel guide rates this crossing among the best street photography spots in the city. On weekends the area is packed with locals and visitors, which adds life to your photos but means you should keep out of people's way and shoot from the pavement. If you have time for a second scene, Jalan Alor is a lively night food street, and Changkat Bukit Bintang has older shophouses and murals in a calmer setting.
text.geographic_location: In the Golden Triangle of central Kuala Lumpur, on Jalan Bukit Bintang beside the Pavilion Kuala Lumpur mall. The KLCC area lies to the north-east.
text.directions_text: From the KLCC area, head south-west towards Jalan Bukit Bintang and ask for Pavilion Kuala Lumpur. Then walk to the pedestrian crossing by its entrance. Look for the busy junction beside the mall frontage. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the crossing and the mall frontage. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is too crowded to step back. Use 2x or more to pick out single walkers or signs without moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Jalan Bukit Bintang and Jalan Sultan Ismail (crossing by the Pavilion Kuala Lumpur entrance; exact corner inferred from the page's 'busy intersection near Lot 10' and 'pedestrian crossing near Pavilion' descriptions). Pedestrians, traffic light trails and neon-lit mall frontage in the busiest part of the district, framed from the street at night. Stand on the pavement at the kerb beside the Jalan Bukit Bintang crossing near the Pavilion Kuala Lumpur entrance, and shoot across towards the crossing and the mall frontage. From here the photo shows pedestrians, traffic light trails and the neon-lit mall frontage in the busiest part of the district. Do not stand in the road, and cross only when the signal allows.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the crossing in the lower third, with the lit frontage filling the background. Wait for a group of people to step into the gap so they become the subject. For a second scene, try Jalan Alor for food-street neon, or Changkat Bukit Bintang for shophouses and murals.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Use night mode after dark and brace your elbows against your body to keep it steady. Tap on the brightest sign to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the neon does not burn out. Try a Live Photo to capture the movement of people and traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the neon signs and mall lights are on and the traffic trails show up. Weekends are the busiest and give the liveliest crowds.

text.access_note: This is an open public street and pavement; if you want to photograph inside Pavilion or another mall, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Traffic and signs are lit after dark, which gives light trails and neon colour at the crossing.
Some phones offer a long-exposure effect for Live Photos that can smooth traffic trails.
Night mode works best when the phone is held steady, for example with elbows braced against the body.
Pedestrians cross at this spot when the signal allows, so stand on the pavement and not in the road.

name: Independence Square
label: Merdeka Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dataran Merdeka' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Independence Square (Kuala Lumpur)'.
notes: Historic square with one of the world's tallest flagpoles.

text.description:
Independence Square, known in Malay as Dataran Merdeka, is a broad green lawn in the middle of old Kuala Lumpur. It was once the Padang, the cricket field of the Selangor Club. It was here at midnight on 30 to 31 August 1957 that the British flag came down and the Malayan flag went up for the first time. A 95-metre flagpole stands at the southern end, one of the tallest in the world, and a round black marble plaque marks the spot where the new flag was raised.

It photographs well because the open grass gives you a clean foreground, and the old government buildings sit along one side. The Sultan Abdul Samad Building, built in an Indo-Saracenic style and housing the government offices from 1897, is the one most visitors want in the frame. The flagpole gives the scene a strong vertical line against all that horizontal lawn.

For a phone, the easiest picture is the wide one: lawn, flagpole and building together. Walk a few steps to the side if you want fewer people in the shot. Early morning or late afternoon usually brings softer light and a quieter square. The Sultan Abdul Samad Building has been reported as under renovation, so some of its facade may be covered in scaffolding. Access to the square has also been reported as restricted at times, so check before you set out.
text.geographic_location: Independence Square is in the historic centre of Kuala Lumpur, on the west side of the Klang River, directly in front of the Sultan Abdul Samad Building. It sits close to Masjid Jamek, the Kuala Lumpur City Gallery and St Mary's Anglican Cathedral.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Masjid Jamek LRT Station, and the square is a short walk to the west of it. Head west from the station and look for the flagpole and the long Sultan Abdul Samad Building. A taxi to Dataran Merdeka also works. From the middle of the square, the phone icon on the map is about 2 minutes on foot to the north. The phone icon on the map is about 100 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the lawn, the flagpole and the building in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the top of the flagpole or the building's details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 100 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Face south across the field toward the flagpole. If you want a different angle, the far south end of the square gives a view back at the building, with the flagpole rising in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the flagpole on one of the vertical lines so it does not split the picture down the middle. Keep the horizon level, because the long building front shows any tilt. Include a strip of lawn in the foreground for depth. From the far south end, a broad view across the whole square shows the old building looking small against the modern towers behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky stays blue and the facade keeps its detail. If the scaffolding bothers you, a tighter zoom on the clean parts of the building can help.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there are fewer people around.

text.access_note: Dataran Merdeka is normally an open public square, but parts of it have been reported closed off at times, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Independence Square is in the historic centre of Kuala Lumpur, close to Masjid Jamek.
Setting the flagpole on a gridline and including foreground lawn will give a more balanced phone photo.
Lowering the exposure slider slightly helps keep the sky and facade detail on a bright day.

name: Thean Hou Temple
label: Thean Hou Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Thean Hou Temple' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/453802547: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Thean Hou Temple' (92 m across).
notes: Colourful six-tiered Chinese temple on a hill.

text.description:
Thean Hou Temple is a six-tiered Chinese temple to the sea goddess Mazu (Tian Hou), built by the Hainanese community in Malaysia. It was completed in 1987 and officially opened in 1989. It is one of the largest temples in Southeast Asia, and it suits a phone camera because so much of it is colourful and close at hand. Red pillars, layered roofs, carvings and rows of hanging lanterns give you plenty to frame in a single shot.

The phone icon on the map is in the lantern courtyards, which several guides describe as the most photographed part of the temple. Stand under the lanterns and point your phone upward. The lanterns fill the frame, and the ornate roofline sits behind them. It is a simple shot, and it works well even if you have never thought much about composition.

If you have time, there are two more pictures worth taking. From the terraces you can catch the temple's tiered red roofs in the foreground, with the Kuala Lumpur skyline behind. In the grounds you will also find the twelve zodiac animal statues, which are good for close-ups and low-angle shots with roofs or greenery behind.

The temple is a working place of worship, so be considerate. Keep flash off near the prayer halls and do not photograph worshippers close-up. Some displays and murals change over time, so treat any older photos you have seen as a guide rather than a promise.
text.geographic_location: Thean Hou Temple stands on top of Robson Heights, on the hill above Jalan Syed Putra, a little way from the Brickfields side of Kuala Lumpur. The address is 65 Persiaran Endah, off Jalan Syed Putra.
text.directions_text: There is no direct public transport to the temple door. The nearest bus stop is at Balai Polis Brickfields, about a 20-minute uphill walk. The road up is steep, so allow extra time and wear comfortable shoes. Once you are inside the grounds, the lantern courtyards are the first place to stop for photos. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) in the lantern courtyards, so the lanterns and roofline fit into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for general views of the courtyards and buildings. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved details, roof ornaments and the zodiac statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Plant your feet in a clear spot under the lanterns and shoot upward. The rows of red lanterns fill the frame, with the ornate roofline behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Tilt the phone up and turn on gridlines. Line up one row of lanterns with a vertical grid line, so the picture feels ordered rather than cluttered. Keep the roofline in the top third of the frame. For a different shot, go to the terraces for the red roofs with the city skyline behind, or get low beside the zodiac statues and shoot up at them against the roofs or greenery.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a lantern to set focus, then slide the exposure slider down a little so the reds stay rich and the sky does not wash out. Keep flash off. In the evening, when the lanterns are lit, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a pillar or your chest while it captures.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning around opening time usually brings soft light and fewer people. In the evening, when the lanterns are lit, they glow. The lantern displays look their best during festivals such as Chinese New Year, though expect more people then.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, and entry is free; check the official site before you go for current hours, dress expectations and any closed areas.
claims_not_in_sources: Ultra-wide (0.5x) helps fit more lanterns and roofline into the frame in a courtyard.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep the red colours rich and avoids a washed-out sky.
Night mode works best if the phone is held steady, for example against a pillar.
Festival periods such as Chinese New Year are likely to be busier.

name: Kuala Lumpur Tower
label: KL Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Taman Tasik Titiwangsa' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Taman Tasik Titiwangsa' (way/487114579): edge nearest the subject (1157 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/5839389988: the OpenStreetMap point 'Kuala Lumpur Tower'.
notes: Telecommunications tower on Bukit Nanas with a viewing deck.

text.description:
Kuala Lumpur Tower, known locally as KL Tower or Menara Kuala Lumpur, is a 421-metre telecommunication tower. Its slim shaft and pod make it easy to pick out on the skyline. The most useful ground-level photo here is not taken at its base, which sits on a hill and is awkward to shoot from. Instead, head to the lake at Taman Tasik Titiwangsa, where the tower stands in the distance and the water can mirror it along with the skyline around it. It is also usually quieter than the tower's own entrance area.

A few facts help you tell the story in your photo. The tower opened to the public on 23 July 1996, when it was the tallest structure in Malaysia. Three years later the Petronas Twin Towers overtook it. It is still the highest viewpoint in the city that the public can visit, and a revolving restaurant sits up in the pod.

From the park the tower is a small, distant shape, so the lake and sky do much of the work. Look for a calm patch of water and keep the tower off-centre, with some shoreline or trees in the foreground. If you want a different angle, KL Forest Eco Park has a treetop walkway where the tower can be seen rising above the canopy. Sunrise and sunset are the times recommended for the lake.
text.geographic_location: The tower stands in central Kuala Lumpur on a hill, near Jalan Bukit Nanas. The reflection viewpoint, Taman Tasik Titiwangsa, is a lakeside park to the north of it.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this viewpoint, so check a local map app for the best way to reach Taman Tasik Titiwangsa from central Kuala Lumpur. Once at the lake, walk along the shore and look south for the tower. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the distant tower closer. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a wider shot with more lake and skyline. Avoid the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the tower itself, as it will shrink to a tiny sliver.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Taman Tasik Titiwangsa. The tower reflected in the park's large central lake, with the skyline around it. From the water's edge you can see the tower reflected in the lake with the skyline around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines rather than in the middle. Keep a good strip of water in the lower half so the reflection fills the foreground. If a branch or shoreline is nearby, let it frame one edge. For a different view of the tower, KL Forest Eco Park offers it above the forest canopy from its treetop walkway.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the tower does not wash out. Wipe your lens first, as distant shots show every smudge. Hold the phone with both hands, or rest it on a rail, to keep zoomed shots sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise and sunset are the recommended times at the lake.

text.access_note: Taman Tasik Titiwangsa is a public park, but check the official site before you go for any local rules or closures.

name: Petaling Street
label: Petaling Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kwai Chai Hong' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kwai Chai Hong' (way/801320516): middle (43 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/446256442: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Petaling Street' (364 m across).
notes: Chinatown's busy market street with a green roof and gate.

text.description:
Petaling Street is Kuala Lumpur's Chinatown, a pedestrianised market street under a green roof, with a Chinese arch at each end. The roof and arches date from a makeover in 2003. In Cantonese the street is called Chee Cheong Kai, meaning Starch Factory Street, after a tapioca mill opened here by the Chinese Kapitan Yap Ah Loy. Today it is lined with stalls, shophouses and food sellers, and it is usually busy with locals and visitors. Haggling is a common sight.

Restored shophouses, wall murals and red lanterns overhead make a tidier picture than the crowded market. The alley has six murals with QR codes that tell of residents' lives in earlier times.

For a second shot, walk to Jalan Petaling and shoot along the lantern-hung street with the stalls and shoppers on both sides. Lorong Petaling 2 is a side lane with large murals, and the Merdeka 118 tower shows in the background. The lanterns may not be up all year, and weekends and holidays are very crowded, so go early or in the evening if you can.
text.geographic_location: In the heart of Kuala Lumpur's Chinatown, a short walk from Central Market and Jamek Mosque.
text.directions_text: Go to Chinatown in central Kuala Lumpur, near Central Market. From there, follow the lanes towards Lorong Panggung and the lantern alley. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the narrow alley so the lanterns, murals and shophouse walls all fit. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. On Jalan Petaling, the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) can pick out one lantern, a stall or a face from further back.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kwai Chai Hong (entrance on the Petaling Street side, in the lantern alley). A narrow back alley of restored shophouses with murals on the walls and red lanterns strung overhead, with Petaling Street's market noise just around the corner. At the entrance on the Petaling Street side, in the lantern alley. From there you can shoot along the narrow lane of restored shophouses, with the murals on the walls and the red lanterns strung overhead.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the alley's centre with the middle grid line, so the lanterns lead the eye along it. Keep the phone level to stop the walls leaning. If the alley is busy, wait a moment for a gap between people. For a different view, try Jalan Petaling for the lantern-hung market street, or Lorong Petaling 2 for the big murals.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a lantern to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the red stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out. In the evening, night mode helps. Hold the phone steady against a wall or your body while it takes the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 10 am or after 5 pm. In the evening the lanterns are lit against the sky.

text.access_note: Petaling Street is an open pedestrian street, and Kwai Chai Hong is described as free to visit, but check the official site before you go for any current restrictions or closures.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit a narrow alley and its overhead lanterns into one frame.
Night mode helps with the lit lanterns in the evening.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep the red of the lanterns rich against a bright sky.

name: Kuala Lumpur Bird Park
label: KL Bird Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Flamingo Pond' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Flamingo Pond' (relation/21406748): middle (48 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/21406759: large area 'Kuala Lumpur Bird Park' (712 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description: Kuala Lumpur Bird Park is a public aviary of about 8.5 hectares (20.9 acres), and it is one of the world's largest covered bird parks. More than 3,000 birds from over 200 species live under its netted canopy. Roughly nine in ten are local birds, and the rest come from places such as Australia, China and Tanzania. It was first planned in 1987 and sits beside the Perdana Botanical Gardens. For a phone camera, the best first stop is Flamingo Pond, close to the main entrance. Flamingos and pelicans wade in the water with thick greenery behind them, so you get colour and a natural backdrop without much effort. Several visitor guides name it as the park's best photo spot, and there is a kiosk nearby if you want a break. Two other places are worth a look. The Waterfall Aviary is a walk-through aviary with a waterfall and lake behind the birds, and you can walk behind the waterfall for a different angle. One guide names a Love Aviary with colourful parrots, flamingos and storks close enough to photograph without zooming; its name on site may differ, so check the park map. Overhead netting shows up in some shots, so check the top of your frame before you press the button. Professional or commercial photography may need a special permit, and drones are reportedly not allowed.
text.geographic_location: In central Kuala Lumpur, next to the Perdana Botanical Gardens, the Kuala Lumpur Butterfly Park, the National Mosque and the Royal Malaysian Police Museum.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Perdana Botanical Gardens area next to the park and follow signs to the Bird Park's main entrance. Flamingo Pond is just inside the park, near that entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the pond, so the birds and the greenery behind them both fit. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for single birds, and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the walk-through aviary or by the waterfall to show the whole scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (inside the park, near the main entrance). Flamingos and pelicans wading in the pond, with greenery behind them that works as a backdrop. Flamingo Pond is inside the park near the main entrance. Stand at the pond's edge and look across the water at the flamingos and pelicans wading, with greenery behind them as a backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the birds on one of the lines, leaving the green backdrop behind them. Keep the netting out of the top of the frame by tilting the phone slightly down. If you have time, the Waterfall Aviary and the Love Aviary (if it appears under that name on site) make good alternatives, with the waterfall and lake or the colourful parrots as your subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bird to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the water looks bright. Try portrait mode on a single bird to soften the background. Live Photos can catch a wing flap or a bird turning its head.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No single best time is set for this spot. The park has shade, so it should work through the day. Earlier in the day may be quieter and the birds livelier.

text.access_note: This is a fenced, covered park, and professional photography may need a permit, so check the official site for entry details and any photography permit rules before you go.

name: Sri Maha Mariamman Temple
label: Sri Mahamariamman
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jalan Tun H.S. Lee' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Jalan Tun H.S. Lee nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1248817862: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sri Mahamariamman Temple' (69 m across).
notes: Oldest Hindu temple in the city with a colourful gopuram.

text.description:
Sri Maha Mariamman is the oldest Hindu temple in Kuala Lumpur. It was founded in 1873 and moved to its present site beside Chinatown in 1885. The reason to stop with a phone is the gopuram, the gateway tower. It rises in five tiers to 22.9 m and is covered in painted figures of Hindu gods, with 228 idols credited to a team led by the sculptor S. T. Muniappa from Tamil Nadu. The tower was finished in 1972, and the temple was consecrated the following year.

The tower is tall and narrow, so it suits a portrait-orientation frame. The best view is from the opposite side of Jalan Tun H.S. Lee, where you can stand back far enough to fit the whole tower in with the street in front. Everyday details add life to the shot, such as worshippers with garlands walking through the gate. If you want something closer, a second view is from the temple entrance itself, looking up at the crowded tiers of painted sculptures.

Be considerate. Photography is generally fine in the outer areas but is restricted in the inner sanctum and during ceremonies. It is polite to ask before photographing worshippers. The temple gets very busy at festivals such as Deepavali and Thaipusam, so allow extra time and patience on those days.
text.geographic_location: The temple is on Jalan Tun H.S. Lee at the edge of Chinatown in central Kuala Lumpur. Its address is 163, Jalan Tun H.S. Lee.
text.directions_text: Head for the edge of Chinatown and look for the tall, colourful gopuram on Jalan Tun H.S. Lee. Cross to the opposite pavement. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the road so the whole tower fits. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if traffic or people stop you from backing off far enough, or for the close-up from the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jalan Tun H.S. Lee (opposite sidewalk from the temple entrance, set back about 10 m). The full 22.9 m gopuram tower filling a portrait-orientation frame, with the street in the foreground. Stand on Jalan Tun H.S. Lee, on the opposite pavement from the temple entrance and set back a little. From here the full gopuram fills a portrait frame, with the street in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and switch on the gridlines. Keep the phone level so the tower's sides stay straight, and move backwards rather than tilting upwards. Leave a little street at the bottom for depth. For a second picture, go to the temple entrance and shoot upwards at the dense tiers of painted figures, using the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) if you are very close.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try the first 30 minutes after the temple opens. Worshippers with garlands are walking through the gate, and the morning light falls on the figures.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship: photography is fine in the outer areas but restricted in the inner sanctum and during ceremonies, so check the official site for visiting rules and dress expectations before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting a phone upwards makes the sides of a tall building lean inwards, so stepping back and keeping the phone level gives straighter lines.
Traffic or passers-by on the street may sometimes get in the way of the foreground, which is why the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) can help.
The temple is likely to have visiting rules and a dress expectation, as most Hindu temples do.

sources.title: Sri Maha Mariamman Temple, Kuala Lumpur

name: National Mosque of Malaysia
label: National Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Masjid Negara' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/585264338: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Mosque' (253 m across).
notes: Modernist mosque with an umbrella-shaped roof and a tall minaret.

text.description: The National Mosque of Malaysia, known locally as Masjid Negara, was completed in 1965 as a symbol of the country's new independence. It stands in about 13 acres of gardens, and its two best-known features are the 73-metre minaret and the 16-pointed star roof. The roof is meant to recall an open umbrella and the minaret's cap a folded one. The roof was once pink and has been clad in green and blue tiles since the 1987 renovation. Reflecting pools and fountains are spread across the grounds, and they are what make it so rewarding with a phone. From the front pool, the minaret and the folded roof can be mirrored in still water, with fountains and planting around them. Look to the front pool for the minaret's reflection and let it fill the lower half of the frame. If the front pool is busy, the walkways and gardens give a quieter view of the domes and columns, framed by greenery. Photography is allowed outside the prayer hall but not inside it. Visitors dress modestly, and robes are provided at the entrance. The grounds close to tourists during prayer times, so plan your visit around that.
text.geographic_location: In central Kuala Lumpur, close to the Kuala Lumpur railway station and Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin. The mosque grounds are the setting for the photo spot.
text.directions_text: The easiest approach is from the Kuala Lumpur railway station, which is within walking distance of the mosque. There is also an underground passage between the station area and the mosque. The free Go KL City Bus (Red Line) stops at Masjid Negara. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the pool, minaret and roof into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof tiles and minaret details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The front reflecting pool is where to look for the reflection: the 73-metre minaret and the star-shaped roof are mirrored in the still water, with fountains and gardens around them. For a quieter alternative, take a view of the domes and columns framed by the walkway and greenery, away from the crowds at the front pool.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon of the water on the lower third line, so the reflection fills the foreground. Keep the minaret on a vertical line so it doesn't lean. If you want a city backdrop, try a framing that includes Merdeka 118 behind the minaret.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright part of the building to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the white and pale surfaces keep their detail. Hold the phone low and close to the water's edge to strengthen the reflection. Take a few frames, because passing ripples can blur the mirror effect.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light. Late morning or early afternoon suits the fountains, with a balance of light and shadow. Whichever you choose, check the official site for visitor times first, as the grounds close to tourists during prayer times.

text.access_note: The mosque is a place of worship: dress modestly (robes are provided at the entrance), photography is not allowed inside the prayer hall, and tourist access pauses at prayer times, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Holding the phone low near the water's edge strengthens the reflection.
Passing ripples from wind or fountains can break up the mirrored image.
Gridlines help keep the minaret vertical and the horizon level.
The mosque is in central Kuala Lumpur.
Merdeka 118 can be included behind the minaret from the grounds (from the researched viewpoint notes).

name: Sultan Abdul Samad Building
label: Sultan Abdul Samad
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dataran Merdeka' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Dataran Merdeka' (way/23069513): middle (324 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/801337963: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sultan Abdul Samad Building' (247 m across).
notes: Moorish-style colonial building with a clock tower.

text.description:
The Sultan Abdul Samad Building is the old government office block of British-era Kuala Lumpur. It was built between 1894 and 1897 in red brick with white plastered bands and rows of arches. Three copper-clad onion domes crown it, and the tallest sits on a 41-metre clock tower that was designed to echo Big Ben. The front runs for about 137 metres along Jalan Raja, so it is wide as well as tall. Both shapes suit a phone screen: the long line of arches, the domes and the tower all fit into one frame once you have the open square in front of you.

This is the clearest, least obstructed view of the building. The lawn also keeps people and traffic out of your lower frame. The flagpole in the square, which is 95 metres tall, makes a good leading line if you want something in the foreground. For a different shot, move close to the building and frame the clock tower through the arches. From there the modern 118 tower can appear in the same picture.

The building was restored in 2026, including its tower spires. Parts of the façade may still have scaffolding or screens, so look at the building before you plan your shot.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Kuala Lumpur, on Jalan Raja, facing the open lawn of Dataran Merdeka (Merdeka Square) and close to the Royal Selangor Club.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so head to Dataran Merdeka on foot or by whatever local transport suits you. From there the building is to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot. Keep the façade in front of you as you walk, so you can see the whole building before you choose your shot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the far side of the square. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the façade will not fit. Use 2x-3x telephoto, if your phone has it, for the clock tower and domes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Dataran Merdeka (opposite (western) side of the square, facing the building's façade). The full copper-domed, arched façade and clock tower of the building framed across the open lawn of the square. From here the full copper-domed, arched façade and the clock tower are framed across the open lawn.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the horizontal bands of the building up with them, so the façade does not lean. Put the clock tower roughly in the centre and leave some lawn in the lower part of the picture. For a variation, stand so the 95-metre flagpole leads the eye towards the building. Another option is to go up close and frame the clock tower through the arches, where the 118 tower can also appear.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick façade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the domes keep their colour. Use panorama mode only if the building will not fit in a single frame, and hold the phone upright and steady as you sweep. If a vertical shot is better, tilt the phone and keep the tower straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the light is soft and there are fewer people about. Golden hour and evening are also good. Check on site whether the building is lit at night. Night mode helps for evening shots, but hold the phone steady.

text.access_note: Dataran Merdeka is an open public square. The building has galleries, exhibition spaces and cafés, but access to the interior, terrace and opening times may vary, so check the official site before you go. Flying a drone nearby is restricted, so check with the local authorities first.

name: Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia
label: Islamic Arts Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/659878360: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia' (191 m across).
notes: Large museum with domes and ornate tiled interiors.

text.description:
The Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia is the largest museum of Islamic arts in Southeast Asia. It opened on 12 December 1998 and holds more than seven thousand artefacts from across the Islamic world. From a photographer's point of view, the building itself is the draw. The walls have clean, modern lines, and they are set off by turquoise-tiled domes and an entrance reminiscent of an iwan, decorated by Iranian tile workers. The domes have made it a recognisable landmark on the Kuala Lumpur skyline.

The pattern and colour of the tilework give you plenty to shoot. Start with a wide frame of the whole façade and entrance, then move in for close-ups of the tile patterns and the curve of a dome against the sky. Use the gridlines in your camera app to keep the vertical walls straight, and stand square-on to the entrance so the symmetry works for you. Inside, the museum has twelve galleries over two levels, including architecture, manuscripts, textiles, jewellery and a restored early-nineteenth-century Ottoman Room. Rules on photography inside can differ from gallery to gallery, so check the official site and any signs before you take your phone out indoors.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Kuala Lumpur, within walking distance west of Kuala Lumpur railway station.
text.directions_text: The museum is within walking distance west of Kuala Lumpur railway station, so head west on foot from the station. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the façade and entrance. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the domes will not fit. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for tile patterns and the tops of the domes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Move to a spot outside the building where the façade and entrance fit in one frame, and stand square to the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the walls and entrance with them so the verticals stay straight. Take one wide shot of the whole building, then a closer shot of the entrance and its tilework. For the domes, tilt the phone up only a little, and use 2x or more instead of getting closer, to limit the leaning-walls effect.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the turquoise tiles to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. Tap again on a shaded area if the entrance looks too dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is best for showing off the turquoise tiles. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the entrance.

text.access_note: This is a museum, so access and entry rules for the building and its galleries may apply; check the official site before you go.

name: Jamek Mosque
label: Jamek Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dataran Merdeka' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Dataran Merdeka' (way/23069513): middle (324 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/480717734: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jamek Mosque' (216 m across).
notes: Old mosque at the meeting of the Klang and Gombak rivers.

text.description:
Jamek Mosque stands where the Klang and Gombak rivers meet, and that setting is a big part of why it photographs so well. Arthur Benison Hubback designed it in the Indo-Saracenic style, and it opened on 23 December 1909. It was the first large mosque built in Kuala Lumpur and served as the city's main mosque until Masjid Negara opened in 1965. The two main minarets have pink and white banding, which stands out against the greenery and the modern towers nearby. There are three domes, and the tallest rises to about 21.3 metres.

The classic view is from Dataran Merdeka. The clock tower, the historic Sultan Abdul Samad Building and the heritage buildings around the square form part of the surrounding scene. Guides call this the postcard angle, and the nearby bridge was built low so it would not block it. If you have time, the Masjid Jamek Lookout Point @ River of Life shows the mosque and its domes in front of the river junction, with the skyline behind it. The Masjid Jamek Pedestrian Bridge shows the mosque with the river in the foreground.

Visitors cannot go in during prayers, so stay outside and keep to the exterior during services. Opinions differ on the best light. Some people prefer early morning, others sunset or night, and midday sun is harsh.
text.geographic_location: In central Kuala Lumpur, at the meeting point of the Klang and Gombak rivers, reached from Jalan Tun Perak. It sits between Chinatown and Little India, close to Dataran Merdeka.
text.directions_text: Take the train to Masjid Jamek LRT station, which is just outside the mosque compound. It is served by the Kelana Jaya Line, the Sri Petaling Line and the Ampang Line. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the mosque together with the Sultan Abdul Samad Building. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square and sky. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the domes and the banded minarets.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Dataran Merdeka (field area, aiming back at the clock tower side). The mosque framed with the historic Sultan Abdul Samad Building and the city's heritage architecture in the surrounding square. Treat the clock tower and the Sultan Abdul Samad Building as part of the surrounding scene, not the direction you aim. Your photo shows the mosque with the heritage architecture around the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the mosque on one of the thirds, with the historic building filling the other side. Keep your phone level so the minarets stay upright. For a different view, try the River of Life lookout point or the pedestrian bridge. The lookout shows the mosque and its domes in front of the river junction with the skyline behind it. The pedestrian bridge shows the mosque with the river in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mosque to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly to keep the sky and any lit areas from washing out. After dark, hold the phone steady and let night mode work, or brace your arms against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Night is the most recommended time, when the central clock tower is lit up. Early morning and sunset are also popular. Avoid midday, when the sun is harsh.

text.access_note: The mosque is a place of worship and visitors cannot enter during prayers, so stay outside and keep to the exterior; check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.
claims_not_in_sources: Dataran Merdeka is an open public square that is free to enter.
Visitors to a mosque are usually expected to dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees.
Night mode on a phone gives better results if the phone is held steady or braced.

name: Kuala Lumpur railway station
label: KL Railway Station
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin' (4 web pages); placed at the stretch of Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/6762797327: the OpenStreetMap point 'Kuala Lumpur'.

text.description:
Kuala Lumpur railway station is a white, Moorish-style building with arches, domes and little pavilion-topped towers, and it is one of the most distinctive old buildings in the city centre. It was designed by Arthur Benison Hubback, a British architect, and built in the 1910s as a blend of Eastern and Western ideas. For decades it was the city's main railway hub. Long-distance trains moved to KL Sentral in 2001, but the old station still works as a KTM Komuter stop. It sits close to the similarly styled Railway Administration Building, the National Mosque and the Dayabumi Complex, so it fits well into a walk around the area.

It photographs well because the front is long, symmetrical and full of repeating arches. The best view is from across the road, which lets you fit in the whole width and the domes above. The facade faces west, so the light is at its warmest in the late afternoon and evening. The road in front is busy, so wait for a gap in traffic and keep your phone steady. Photography is fine outside, but the station displays a notice saying permission is needed for photos inside the station area, so ask before shooting interiors.
text.geographic_location: In central Kuala Lumpur, on Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin, close to the Railway Administration Building, the National Mosque and the Dayabumi Complex. The Klang River lies between it and Pasar Seni.
text.directions_text: The nearest named station is Pasar Seni (LRT and MRT), about 400 m away across the Klang River. Otherwise, come by taxi and ask for Kuala Lumpur railway station on Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straight, symmetrical view of the facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the whole width will not fit, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the domes and arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin (directly opposite the station's front facade, on the street side). The white Moorish-style facade with its arches and domes, framed across the road from the station entrance. Face east. You will see the white Moorish-style facade with its arches and domes framed across the road from the station entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the building up with the middle line so the symmetry shows. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. For a variation, try the view across the road from the Malayan Railway Administration Building, where its own arches frame the station. A closer, quieter angle on the front walkway is possible from the exit side of the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the walls keep their detail. In traffic, wait for a gap before taking the shot. If you take a Live Photo, the passing traffic is captured as well.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or evening, when the low western sun lights the facade. In the evening, try night mode with your phone braced against something solid.

text.access_note: The outside of the station can be photographed from the public street, but permission is needed for photos inside the station area, so check before you go in. The station is a working KTM commuter stop.
claims_not_in_sources: Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail on a white facade in bright light.
Ultra-wide (0.5x) helps fit the whole building in when you are standing close to it across the road.
Live Photos will capture moving traffic in front of the station.

name: National Monument
label: National Monument
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Perdana Botanical Garden' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Perdana Botanical Garden: Planetarium Negara entrance' (node/6246450817): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1212049483: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Monument' (17 m across).
notes: Bronze sculpture honouring the fallen soldiers.

text.description:
The National Monument (Tugu Negara) honours the people who died in Malaysia's struggle for freedom, mainly against the Japanese occupation in the Second World War and during the Malayan Emergency of 1948 to 1960. The bronze sculpture group stands about 15 metres tall and shows seven figures: five representing the allied forces (one holding the flag, one with a rifle and bayonet, one with a machine gun, and soldiers tending a wounded compatriot) and two lying on the ground representing the defeated communist forces. It was designed by the sculptor Felix de Weldon, cast in Rome and opened on 8 February 1966. It is described as the world's tallest freestanding bronze sculpture grouping.

This map spot is a wider view rather than a close-up. From here the sculpture is a small feature in a green setting of Lake Gardens trees, which gives a calmer, more relaxed picture than the head-on shots taken at the monument itself. At this distance the monument will look small, so use the zoom and keep the greenery in the frame.

If you want the figures filling the picture, walk on to Plaza Tugu Negara. There you can shoot head-on with the reflecting pool in front, or from behind with the tiled pool, the water-lily sculptures and the domed pavilion around the scene.
text.geographic_location: The monument is in the Lake Gardens area of Kuala Lumpur, close to the Malaysian Houses of Parliament.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot; travel to the Lake Gardens area and navigate to the Perdana Botanical Garden. Follow the garden paths in that direction, and check the current state of the area around the monument before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the whole garden scene, then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the monument closer. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a sweeping shot of the lawn and trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Perdana Botanical Garden (lawns and paths across from the monument, looking back toward it). The monument seen at a distance across the greenery of the Lake Gardens, giving a wider setting than the close-up views. From here the sculpture is seen across the greenery of the Lake Gardens, a wider setting than the close-up views.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the monument on a third, with trees or a path leading towards it. Keep plenty of green around it so it reads as part of the gardens. For a tighter shot of the figures, Plaza Tugu Negara is the better alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the monument to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the bronze does not turn into a silhouette. Hold the phone steady with both hands when zoomed in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the gardens are calmer and the light is softer.

text.access_note: The Perdana Botanical Garden is generally free to enter, but the area around the monument may be restricted or under works, so check the official site before you go.

name: Kuala Lumpur City Gallery
label: KL City Gallery
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dataran Merdeka' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Dataran Merdeka' (way/23069513): middle (324 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4283481889: the OpenStreetMap point 'Kuala Lumpur City Gallery'.
notes: Colonial building next to Merdeka Square with the 'I Love KL' sign.

text.description:
Kuala Lumpur City Gallery is a handsome late-Victorian building on Jalan Raja, on the edge of Merdeka Square. It was completed in 1898 and designed by A. C. Norman, the government architect of the Federated Malay States. It was built as the government printing office, which is why it looks like an official building rather than a museum. It became the City Gallery in 1989. Inside, the ground floor has the "Memories of Kuala Lumpur" exhibition of old photographs and maps. Upstairs there is a large model of the city with a light and sound show.

It photographs well because the building sits right beside the open square, with the historic enclave and the flagpole around it. That lets you take it in context rather than just as a facade. From the lawn side of the square you can fit the gallery, the open space in front and some of the surrounding heritage buildings into one frame. For the classic tourist picture, walk over to the large red I LOVE KL sign, which puts the gallery's facade behind the lettering.

The square view is a wider scene, not a close-up of the facade, so step closer if you want detail. Inside, the model room is darkened and you can only enter at the start of the show, so plan your photos around that.
text.geographic_location: The gallery is on Jalan Raja in central Kuala Lumpur, facing Merdeka Square (Dataran Merdeka), in the city's historic enclave. It is a short walk from the square's flagpole and the Sultan Abdul Samad Building.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Merdeka Square (Dataran Merdeka) in central Kuala Lumpur. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the lawn so the building keeps a natural shape and the square stays in the frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the I LOVE KL sign and want the whole facade behind it. Use 2x to pick out the roofline and architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Dataran Merdeka (the open lawn side facing the gallery on Jalan Raja). The gallery building across the open square, with the historic enclave and flagpole in the wider frame. On the open lawn side facing the gallery on Jalan Raja. From here the gallery building sits across the open square, to the south, with the historic enclave and the flagpole in the wider view. For the classic alternative, use the I LOVE KL monument, which puts the red sign in the foreground and the gallery's facade behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the gallery on one of the vertical lines, leaving open lawn in the foreground and the flagpole or neighbouring buildings to one side. Keep the phone level so the walls stay upright. For the I LOVE KL picture, crouch slightly and keep the whole sign and the facade in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Weekends are best, as traffic on the road in front of the nearby Sultan Abdul Samad Building is reported to be very light then. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the building.

text.access_note: The square is open public space, but the gallery's opening days and entry arrangements can vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light for photographing the building.
Gridlines help keep walls upright and place the building off-centre in the frame.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in a facade when the sky is bright.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit the sign and the whole facade into one frame at close range.
The gallery is about 3 minutes on foot from the stand-here point, calculated from the distance given.
